title: Transactions, ACID, isolation levels and deadlocks

videos.script: Four lessons of reading, and nothing you typed ever changed a row. This one starts with the three statements that do — insert, update and delete — and with the single property that separates them from everything before it: a wrong one does not rerun. {{writes}} Which is why they waited for this lesson. Every lesson so far has been one statement at a time. This is the lesson about two. {{two}} Move money between accounts and it is a subtraction and an addition. If the machine loses power between them, the money is gone — not misplaced, gone, and no amount of careful code prevents that on its own. {{money}} A transaction is how you say those two statements are one thing. Both, or neither. That part everybody knows, and it is the easy half. {{both}} The hard half is that your two statements are not alone. Somebody else is running theirs at the same time, on the same rows, and what each of you is allowed to see of the other's unfinished work is a setting. It has four values, the default is different on PostgreSQL and MySQL, and almost nobody checks. {{isolation}} There is a class of bug that lives there. Two people book the last seat, each having checked that it was free, and both checks were correct when they ran. The database did nothing wrong and the seat is sold twice. {{seat}} So we do the anomalies first, by name and by example, then the levels that prevent each one, then locking — which is what you reach for when you want to be explicit. {{plan}} And one thing that is not optional: at the strictest level the database will refuse a transaction and tell you to run it again. If your application has no retry loop, you have chosen that level and not implemented it. {{retry}}
